articles.title: PEERSTITCH Malware Deployed via FortiOS Flaw Bypasses Checks on Tagged VPN Sessions
articles.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
articles.content:
A suspected advanced threat actor has been observed exploiting a security flaw in Fortinet FortiOS to deliver a previously unreported memory-resident ARM64 malware known as PEERSTITCH.
The attack involves the exploitation of CVE-2025-61624 (CVSS score: 5.4), a path traversal flaw in the command line interpreter of FortiOS, FortiPAM, FortiProxy, and FortiSwitchManager that could allow a privileged attacker to achieve arbitrary write or delete files via specifically crafted arguments to existing commands. It was patched by Fortinet in April 2026.
"PEERSTITCH leaves no persistent binary on disk, opens no listening ports and initiates no outbound network connections," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 researchers Daniel Gott and Shawn Westfall said. "Instead, it communicates through traffic generated by legitimate processes on the infected host, which makes the malware resistant to conventional endpoint and network detection."
The cybersecurity company said it discovered the activity as part of its prolonged network intrusion against a telecommunications managed service provider that took place in September 2024. The multi-stage network intrusion is being tracked as CL-STA-0954 (aka UNC5820), with initial access obtained by exploiting a critical Fortinet FortiManager flaw dubbed FortiJump (CVE-2024-47575).
Following a successful compromise of the appliance, the attackers are said to have exfiltrated an archive containing running configurations, cryptographic material, and database files containing information about more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls. Some of the harvested details are listed below -
- The FortiManager appliance's own serial number and its management relationships to every enrolled device
- Running configuration files for more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls across internal infrastructure and client networks
- Central management SQLite databases
- An inventory listing more than 500 FortiGate serial numbers alongside their respective public IP addresses
- Internal network topology maps, routing tables and interface configurations
- Ciphertext administrative, local, and SSL/VPN credentials
- Encoded cryptographic trust material, including public certificates, and private keys
The stolen information was then used to conduct network reconnaissance, establish long-term access, intercept network traffic, set up unauthorized FortiGate SSL/VPN sessions to perimeter firewalls, deploy backdoors, and exploit a separate privilege-escalation vulnerability (i.e., CVE-2025-61624) to deploy PEERSTITCH.
The malware is a 64-bit Linux ARM64 executable written in C. It includes an auto-script designed to download five components from an external server ("23.240.77[.]233:8085") -
- pM.js, an environment preparation script (self-deleting)
- a.js (saved as index.js), an Emscripten JavaScript runtime module
- a.wasm (saved as index.wasm), a compiled WebAssembly binary module
- b.js (saved as ipssem.js), a deployment orchestrator script
- dd (saved as lldprx), a native ARM64 ELF binary injector (PEERSTITCH core)
The main phase of the attack begins after an execution delay. The orchestrator ("ipssem.js") launches "lldprx," which then serves as a process memory patching injector targeting two core FortiOS daemons: "/bin/miglogd" and "/bin/iked."
Specifically, it locates the running processes associated with the two daemons, enumerates their memory layout, attaches to them using ptrace and halts their execution using PTRACE_INTERRUPT, allocates executable memory and writes malicious code into it, and redirects execution through the injected code.
The end goal behind this hooking step is to create a "covert, memory-resident communication bridge" between the two legitimate FortiOS processes instead of using a conventional network connection or file, and use them as a cover to sidestep detection.
In particular, the miglogd hook is equipped to recognize a marker in the data passing through the process. This includes two specific markers -
- TCP port marker - 8550 (embedded within traffic data, not a listening port)
- IP address marker - 169.254.0.1 (link-local identifier used for pattern matching)
Once this pattern is identified, it passes the associated session token or identifier to the iked daemon, whose hook later looks for that identifier while handling subsequent VPN sessions. If such a tag exists within that VPN session's injection buffer, it takes an alternative execution path, bypassing default FortiOS security validations.
Put differently, the hooks injected into the two FortiOS processes change how the VPN daemon handles particular sessions.
Besides deploying PEERSTITCH, the attackers have been observed establishing a separate command-and-control (C2) channel by leveraging the native Apache "mod_md" module on FortiGate firewalls in order to spawn an SSH-based reverse shell.
"The attackers also impersonated the FortiManager platform to pull from managed firewalls of other hosts in the targeted network," the researchers said. "The attackers demonstrated proficiency in Fortinet appliance architecture, FortiOS internals and FortiOS management protocols."
Although not definitive, it's suspected that the attackers may have exploited other flaws like CVE-2024-26009 and CVE-2024-26008 to carry out this task. However, Unit 42 emphasized that exploiting these vulnerabilities requires the device to be enrolled in FortiGate Cloud/FortiCloud SSO, which none of the affected firewalls held.
In addition, CL-STA-0954 has been identified as undertaking various measures to remove forensic artifacts through termination of syslog generation, crash log clearing, logging telemetry disruption, and automatic deletion of rogue administrator accounts and auto-script objects after execution.
"This intrusion highlights a growing threat, the weaponization of centralized edge management ecosystems to compromise downstream networks," Unit 42 said. "The discovery of the PEERSTITCH implant demonstrates the increasing technical maturity of edge-device malware."
"By operating as a one-shot injector, avoiding persistent disk artifacts and building a covert inter-process communication bridge inside process memory, the attackers achieved sustained persistence while evading traditional monitoring."
Update
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), on October 16, 2026, added CVE-2025-61624 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by October 19, 2026.
articles.summary:
Threat actors are exploiting a Fortinet FortiOS vulnerability to deploy PEERSTITCH, a sophisticated memory-resident malware that evades detection by operating within legitimate system processes on ARM64 devices.

### Key Points
- Attackers exploited CVE-2025-61624, a path traversal flaw in FortiOS, to inject the PEERSTITCH malware into memory.
- PEERSTITCH avoids disk persistence and network listeners by using a covert communication bridge between the miglogd and iked daemons.
- The intrusion, tracked as CL-STA-0954, began by compromising a FortiManager appliance to steal credentials and configurations for over 500 firewalls.
- The malware uses an Emscripten-based orchestrator to inject malicious code into running processes via ptrace, bypassing standard security validations.
- CISA added CVE-2025-61624 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in October 2026, mandating immediate patching for federal agencies.

### Why it Matters
This campaign demonstrates the increasing technical maturity of attackers targeting centralized edge management ecosystems to gain deep access into downstream networks. By weaponizing legitimate processes and avoiding disk-based artifacts, the malware effectively bypasses traditional endpoint detection and network monitoring tools.

articles.title: This Week in Security: Critical DNS Keys Rotated, Hacking Freezers Isn’t Cool, OpenAI Spies On Itself, and Advanced Hardware Wallet Hacks
articles.author: Mike Kershaw
articles.content:
Critical Internet keys changed this week. Did you notice? The keys behind DNSSEC, the system for cryptographically validating DNS responses, rolled over on October 11 2026. This is the second time the DNSSEC keys have rotated since the system was implemented, and the first time in 2018 didn’t exactly go entirely smoothly.
DNS is what resolves a host name and turns it into an IP address. It underpins web browsing, email, and just about every other connection. It’s also a very early Internet protocol, written in both a simpler, less paranoid era, and an era where encryption was computationally expensive and legally problematic. DNS offers little protection against malicious actors spoofing responses, and the impacts range from phishing to redirecting email to just about any other manipulation of connections you can image.
DNSSEC addresses this by creating a chain of trust between DNS resolvers — the servers that forward the DNS query into the DNS infrastructure and return the results — and the global DNS servers. Part of this chain of trust is the root key that each resolver must have and trust, and this key is what changed this week. DNSSEC resolvers automatically watch for a new root of trust key, but the key must be signed by the previous root of trust, and is checked for at least 30 days before it is trusted. If someone were able to issue a bogus certificate, they would have to maintain control of the infrastructure for over a month before DNS resolvers would trust it.
The process of distributing the new key actually began more than a year ago, on January 11, 2025, to give DNSSEC resolvers time to get the new key. DNSSEC services should have had plenty of time to obtain and trust the new key, and unless DNS stopped working for you this week, they did their job.
The next major change for DNSSEC will require more profound changes to deploy a new signing algorithm that will be post-quantum secure.
Ransomware Recovery Company Didn’t Recover
BleepingComputer reports that the CEO of a company advertising services for recovering from ransomware attacks has been charged with fraud.
The company advertised that it could help with recovering from a ransomware attack by providing decryption services to unlock the ransomed files. Instead, the CEO of the company is accused of negotiating a ransom payment with the attackers and charging the victims a premium on top of the ransom.
In addition to fraudulent claims of decrypting the data without a ransom, this could fall foul of embargo laws against paying ransomware operators in some countries, or be against customer policy regarding payments.
The charges detail incidents in which the ransomware operators were paid $9,800, while the victims were charged $150,000 for “recovery”, and claim the company overall paid more than $8 million in ransom fees while charging customers $18 million.
More Refrigeration Hacks
Several weeks ago, commissaries operated by the United States military suffered a series of refrigeration failures. Units on multiple bases in multiple states and countries entered defrost mode, which activated heaters, spoiling food overnight. This week, hundreds of supermarkets in France have suffered the same issue, with units heating up and some even reportedly catching fire.
The attack started Sunday night, and not only triggers defrost mode, but seems to force the units to stay in defrost mode for a prolonged period. Losses are estimated to reach over $300,000. French prosecutors have called for investigations of the wide-spread attacks.
Clearly, a vulnerability has been found in the refrigeration controllers connected to the Internet, and fingers are being pointed at the Danfoss brand, which is also used by the US military bases. Researcher Kevin Beaumont points out that it may not even be a traditional vulnerability: Many of the units are directly connected to the Internet, with the username “admin”, and a password that changes daily. Unfortunately, the password changes to the current date. “Every single one is like this. You can just log in and change the temperature. Anybody can do it, easily.”
OpenAI employee charged with spying
An OpenAI employee was charged with spying after being caught placing “sophisticated listening devices” in meeting rooms, hidden in toilet paper: the most sophisticated of camouflage.
Employees discovered the device approximately two days after it was placed, according to the report. Ironically, logs indicate the employee used OpenAI’s own chatbot to help design the device and identify locations for it. Photos of the device look like it a SEEED Studio ESP32 device, a dev board likely very familiar to readers.
Stop & Shop and Hannaford hacked
The US supermarket chains Stop & Shop and Hannaford, which share a common owner, seem to have been hacked. There aren’t many details available yet, but multiple news sources in multiple states are reporting that the stores have taken their websites and online ordering completely offline, however stores remain open.
The company says it does not currently believe that customer payment details were part of the compromise.
Hardware wallets under attack
Kim Zetter brings the report of crypto thefts via hardware implanted in Ledger wallets.
Hardware wallets are offered as the panacea every time another crypto heist or supply-chain stealer makes the rounds. The idea is simple: private keys stay on the device and never touch your daily-driver, which is surely contaminated with keyloggers and trojans. The crypto transaction is built on the host and hands it to the device, the wallet device then solves it with the private keys and returns the signature. The only user interface is typically a screen display, which is exactly where the physical supply chain hack against Ledger happened.
The implants, found mainly in Ledger Nano X devices so far, sit dormant until the owner sets up the wallet. When the device shows the new recovery seed on its screen, the implant reads each character and sends the seed out through its own LTE modem, antenna, and eSIM. The implant never touches the host computer or the users WiFi network. The secure storage inside the wallet is never compromised: the hardware implant spies directly on the LCD to read the recovery keys as displayed to the user.
Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery links about 315 drained accounts, roughly $102 million in Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron and others, to devices sold by CryptoBilis: that’s Ledger’s authorized reseller for Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
[Joe Grand], a hardware hacker often featured here and the force behind many DEFCON conference badges, began looking in August 2025 after a Reddit post from someone who had bought a wallet on a Thai marketplace. [Joe] bought eight more Nano X units and found implants in four of them. This was reported to Ledger in March of 2026, but according to [Grand], Ledger didn’t follow up for months.
Then in September, Mark Karpelès, the former Mt. Gox CEO, published a teardown showing how the implants have evolved. The first generation used hand-soldered wires to the screen. The second used a transparent orange flex circuit laminated onto the board, with a smaller battery to make room. The third uses a black-coated flex with the part numbers scraped off and a custom antenna. A Japan-based researcher who examined ten Nano X and two Flex devices found five distinct implant designs. They traced the eSIM traffic to an Alibaba-managed data center in Hong Kong, with at least 90 implants reporting seeds there in June alone.
Ledger’s official position is that a “limited number” of devices came from a single seller. It says there is no sign that its own systems were compromised, and it has told resellers to buy only through authorized channels and “never to restock returned products. That last line points at a likely route: buy wallets, implant them, return them, and let them go back on the shelf.
Despite the claims of a single compromised seller, a user named [Johannes] found implants in two Nano X units bought at MediaMarkt stores in Europe, and MediaMarkt is a listed authorized reseller with around a thousand stores across ten countries. There are also reports of implanted Flex devices, and Stax reports that are still unverified. Trezor has started trimming its own authorized-seller list as a “preventive step.” Attribution is still unknown.
CryptoBilis changed ownership earlier this year under an NDA that only recently expired, which has raised eyebrows. Zetter is careful to note that there’s no evidence connecting CryptoBilis to the implants or the thefts.
The takeaway is uncomfortable for anyone who has told people to “just buy a hardware wallet”. The threat model always assumed the device itself was trustworthy, and “buy direct from the vendor” was advice for being extra careful. Now it’s the minimum. Tamper-evident packaging clearly isn’t enough against someone with a lamination process and a parts budget. The options get less fun from here: open the case and inspect the board, which voids the warranty, and good luck spotting a black flex on a black PCB, generate the seed somewhere you control and import it, or use multi-signing across vendors so one bad device can’t empty everything.
Crypto forces you to be your own security, and if you have enough money for someone to design an attack that would have only been expected of a nation-state a few years ago, your home-grown security has to be really, really good.
articles.summary:
The global internet infrastructure successfully completed a critical DNSSEC root key rollover on October 11, 2026, marking a significant update to the system’s underlying chain of trust.

### Key Points
- The DNSSEC root key, which validates DNS responses to prevent spoofing, was updated following a year-long distribution process that began in January 2025.
- A ransomware recovery firm CEO faces fraud charges for allegedly charging victims $18 million while secretly paying attackers only $8 million in ransom.
- Internet-connected Danfoss refrigeration controllers were exploited in France and at U.S. military bases, causing food spoilage due to easily guessable "admin" passwords.
- Hardware implants in Ledger Nano X wallets have enabled the theft of approximately $102 million in cryptocurrency by capturing recovery seeds directly from device screens.
- An OpenAI employee was charged with espionage after using the company's own AI to help design and hide listening devices within office meeting rooms.

### Why it Matters
These events highlight the persistent vulnerability of both legacy internet protocols and modern consumer hardware to sophisticated, targeted attacks. As security threats evolve from simple software exploits to complex physical supply-chain tampering, users and organizations must adopt more rigorous verification processes to maintain digital and physical integrity.

articles.title: The Week AI Blinked?
articles.author: David Dayen
articles.content:
This week, Character.AI, a former unicorn startup that allowed users to create virtual companions, announced it was filing for bankruptcy while selling its remaining assets to Disney. Bankruptcy is a convenient way to dodge accountability for the company’s several active lawsuits and investigations into allegations that its chatbots posed as doctors and encouraged children into suicides. The asset purchase is also amusing, since Disney had previously sued Character.AI for deploying its characters for their chatbots.
But bankruptcy also gives a look under the hood at the AI ecosystem, and it’s not a pleasant picture. Character.AI had attracted 12 million active users, but computing costs to handle that user base were exorbitant. The company was losing between $8 million and $9 million a month. Without the capital to finance even more money-losing growth, it resorted to corroding the user experience to reduce costs, both by using cheap substitute models that reduced engagement and by placing usage restrictions on free users. It also introduced advertising and then purchases into its app in a bid to huckster its way out of trouble. The primary effect of all this was turning off core users, a bad sign for a company desperate to increase revenue.

Analysis that goes beyond the noise with in-depth, progressive reporting.
No paywall, no programmatic ads — just the reporting. Unsubscribe anytime. Submitting your email signs you up for The Daily Prospect, our weekday morning newsletter.
While Character.AI’s scale wasn’t near the levels of the industry’s giants, the problem it encountered is familiar. The industry is saddled with a conundrum: Increasing user bases correlates with worsening financials. Unlike the software industry, where each additional copy of Photoshop or Microsoft Word takes almost nothing to produce, AI models are very resource-intensive to run. The more people use the product, the more money it takes to run the system, and in this case at least, setting prices high enough to cover costs craters the customer base. As a result, corners are cut, revenue fillers like ads are introduced, the product becomes crappier and more predatory, users quit anyway, and the company goes under.
This financial mismatch would be one thing if we were talking about a network of gaming apps for phones, or a series of niche hobby shops. It’s another if the industry with this catch-22 is the one that America and the world is reliant on for virtually all economic growth.
The hyperscale giants would insist that they are not trapped by this problem. At a recent investor day event in advance of its anticipated November initial public offering, Anthropic asserted that third-quarter revenue increased 45 percent to $16.8 billion. But even this did not necessarily translate into profits; Anthropic was cagey about it, claiming that it is “profitable after making certain adjustments,” a massaged accounting that simply isn’t credible. The S-1 prospectus that would lay out the actual numbers has yet to be released publicly.
The most equivalent comparable company to Anthropic, OpenAI, last week had to acknowledge that its annualized revenue was $20 billion less than what it had been touting to investors, suggesting that numbers from these companies could be subject to change. The disappointing number for OpenAI came even after the recent addition of ads in ChatGPT, which sounds like the Character.AI pattern.
There’s also no accepted definition of revenue from these companies: Anthropic is including sales by its cloud partners into its own revenue model, but OpenAI isn’t. Given that this is the key figure to determine the viability of the enterprise, this seems like something you’d want to iron out.
OpenAI, for what it’s worth, expects to lose $280 billion between now and 2030, and that’s even after projecting revenue to increase tenfold in that time period. Bain Capital’s analysis, which is likely more conservative than OpenAI’s, shows a $4.2 trillion revenue gap by 2030 across the entire industry. How can that be made up? Integrating ads into chatbots, autonomously operating virtually everything on Earth, using robots for just about every manufacturing process, and coming up with some untold number of new product developments, according to Bain. This is your reminder that 2030 is just over three years away.
By the way, here’s one such new product: OpenAI’s answer to Meta’s Muse companion, which failed almost immediately at the product launch. Muse became a leading app download upon its launch, but it has cooled significantly since then.
Then there is competition from open-source models, which have been consistently only three to six months behind the frontier labs, and can be run on local hardware—a major advantage for any industry with security worries. Open-source competition also weakens the prices AI firms can charge for usage, which was originally their primary strategy to boost revenue.
And the above discussion is focused on the business financials, not the threat to destroy humanity (which is in Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, reportedly) or the industry’s significant legal risk. Eight states—including ones not normally associated with aggressive enforcement like Idaho, Nebraska, West Virginia, and Kansas—just sued OpenAI over releasing ChatGPT models without safeguards to prevent harmful circumstances. The Third Circuit Court of Appeals just rejected a fair use defense for mass AI training on copyrighted material. And the Federal Trade Commission opened an investigation and on Thursday issued subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic over safety incidents like hacking into private and government websites.
The Prospect in your inbox
Analysis that goes beyond the noise with in-depth, progressive reporting.
No paywall, no programmatic ads — just the reporting. Unsubscribe anytime. Submitting your email signs you up for The Daily Prospect, our weekday morning newsletter.
I have less than no expectations for the FTC probe, considering that the same team ended an OpenAI investigation begun during the Biden administration. But there are legitimate risks to these firms and the AI industry in general, and even if you toss them entirely aside, it’s a struggle to make the economics work.
And to be clear, if the economics don’t work for the top frontier model makers, that trickles down to every company reliant upon them. That explains the sinking of AI stocks across the board in recent days, including a 15 percent drop in one session for “neocloud” company CoreWeave, whose debt load has close to doubled to $50 billion in just one quarter, and whose bonds have been beaten down beyond distressed levels. A neocloud is a data center developer that supplies the raw materials, hosts tenants, and manages the financing; if AI demand is high and development is brisk, these should be soaring. But according to Reuters, default insurance for CoreWeave implies “a nearly 63 percent chance of default in five years,” despite an effective guarantee from Nvidia, one of its biggest investors.
To be clear, CoreWeave doesn’t have some special problem relative to other parts of the industry but a version of the same problem: There isn’t enough revenue to go around to make up for the astronomical expense in maintaining the system. Even at current or increased demand levels, it’s hard to pencil out to profitability. One ominous research note from the firm Gartner this week estimated that 80 percent of neoclouds like CoreWeave could fail by 2030. When you think about the ways in which the major tech firms hide AI debt from their own balance sheets, a fall of the neoclouds would be poised to push upward over time.
Perhaps the biggest indicator of a downturn in the industry is the sudden failure of the IPO for Firmus, a $30 billion Australian neocloud company led by someone who was sent to prison for insider trading (!) but was nonetheless backed by some of the biggest companies in AI. It would have been the largest IPO on Australian markets in 30 years, but it vanished in a matter of days. It used to be that you could just throw the name “AI” onto a company and soar on the exchanges; one neocloud called SB Energy filed for an IPO in August without a single data center in operation. But that boom mentality may not be the reality anymore. The Wall Street Journal reported that a recent panel at a data center development conference had the title “Are We Screwed?”
Sam Altman said in an interview last week that “the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.” It appears that those bad things are already here; we’re still waiting on the benefits.
articles.summary:
Character.AI has filed for bankruptcy and is selling its assets to Disney after struggling with high operational costs and mounting legal challenges regarding its virtual companion chatbots.

### Key Points
- Character.AI faced monthly losses of $8 million to $9 million while attempting to support 12 million active users.
- The company is currently embroiled in multiple lawsuits and investigations concerning chatbot safety and the unauthorized use of intellectual property.
- OpenAI and Anthropic face similar financial pressures, with OpenAI projecting $280 billion in losses by 2030 despite aggressive revenue growth targets.
- The "neocloud" sector, including companies like CoreWeave, faces significant default risks as high infrastructure costs outpace revenue generation.
- Gartner analysts estimate that 80% of neocloud data center providers could fail by 2030 due to the industry's unsustainable economic model.

### Why it Matters
The collapse of Character.AI highlights a fundamental economic mismatch where the high cost of running AI models makes scaling difficult without compromising product quality or profitability. This instability threatens the broader tech ecosystem, as investors and companies struggle to reconcile massive infrastructure spending with uncertain long-term revenue streams.

articles.title: A Tesla Flying Car? I Don’t Know, Man
articles.author: Aarian Marshall
articles.content:
Where is my flying car? The enduring question sort of, kind of, might have an answer: In McGregor, Texas.
On Thursday, Tesla showed off a version of its new Roadster 2 sports car in a demonstration at SpaceX’s rocket development testing facility. And in its own way, with an awkward jerking maneuver, the Roadster flew a few dozen feet. The vehicle, which doesn’t yet have a price but is likely to be very expensive, is slated to go into production in 2028. The vehicle didn’t have a human occupant during the demo “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” Tesla CEO Elon Musk said at the event.
Tesla’s Roadster “sort of, kind of, might” be an actual flying car because aviation experts say legally catching air in the vehicle will likely involve plenty of government permissions and red tape.
The Federal Aviation Administration “has jurisdiction over any machine that leaves the surface of the earth,” says Scott Miller, an airline pilot and a lecturer in the Aviation and Technology program at San José State University. The vehicle “is going to introduce a whole set of regulatory issues.”
At the event Thursday, Musk acknowledged as much. “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions," he said. “This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car.”
In a written statement, FAA spokesperson Rick Breitenfeldt said, "The Tesla vehicle does not meet the FAA's definition of an aircraft."
Any flying vehicle that weighs more than 250 or so pounds would need to go through an FAA approval process and require clearance to operate in the national airspace, says Michael McCormick, a former FAA official who now heads the Air Traffic Management program at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Getting that certification, he predicts, could take “at least a year.” Your standard driver's license, meanwhile, wouldn’t cut it. Any Tesla owner piloting such a vehicle would likely have to obtain a recreational aviation license.
Actually taking off and landing the Roadster 2 would likely present its own set of issues. Most states require aircraft to take off from airports or designated helipads. Launching from the road to the air would fall under state or local rules, says Miller, and many places do not look kindly on the concept of sudden aircraft intrusions on their streets and highways. That’s the reason “it’s pretty rare to be able to jump in a helicopter and land at your favorite steakhouse to have a steak,” he says. Drivers might only be able to truly operate the vehicle on a large, private piece of land.
The FAA today is working on rules, regulations, and pilot projects around another sort of “flying car,” or what’s more commonly known as an electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) vehicle. These aircraft use several smaller electric motors and propellers to carry up to four passengers between 20 and 150 miles, sometimes autonomously. The companies building the technology envision them taking off from small, local “vertipads,” allowing riders to skip urban traffic by floating above the fray.
The Trump administration this year launched a limited, three-year pilot project using the aircraft, where companies are able to test the tech in several states. It has taken years for the companies to receive certifications from the federal government.
When it comes to the Roadster 2, there are practical questions, too. True flying cars have struggled to take off because of the physics-led contradiction at the heart of the idea. What makes a car safe and durable enough to operate on roads is weight. But “weight is the enemy of an airplane,” says Miller. “Flying cars haven’t been able to find that balance of power versus weight.”
Still, Miller found himself impressed by Thursday’s demo. “If this does make it into production, that is a truly impressive engineering and production feat,” he says.
Updated on October 16 at 1:50 pm ET: We've added an official statement from the FAA.
articles.summary:
Tesla demonstrated a prototype of its upcoming Roadster 2 sports car at a SpaceX facility in Texas, showcasing the vehicle's ability to briefly hover above the ground.

### Key Points
- Tesla CEO Elon Musk showcased the Roadster 2 at a rocket testing facility in McGregor, Texas, with production currently slated for 2028.
- The demonstration featured an unmanned vehicle performing a short-distance hover, though the car is not yet safety-optimized or commercially available.
- Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials stated the vehicle does not currently meet the legal definition of an aircraft and would require extensive regulatory certification.
- Experts note that operating a flying vehicle would likely require a recreational aviation license and adherence to strict airspace and takeoff regulations.
- Engineering challenges persist, as the weight required for road safety often conflicts with the lightweight design necessary for efficient flight.

### Why it Matters
The demonstration highlights the significant regulatory and engineering hurdles facing the development of consumer-grade flying vehicles. While the technology represents a major feat of innovation, it remains unclear how such vehicles will navigate existing aviation laws and infrastructure constraints.

articles.title: Tokenized Tesla surges as Elon Musk unveils SpaceX-powered flying Roadster prototype
articles.author: Oliver Knight
articles.content:
Tokenized Tesla surges as Elon Musk unveils SpaceX-powered flying Roadster prototype
Volume in Hyperliquid’s Tesla contract hit $47 million in one hour after Elon Musk’s flying Roadster demo, up from $2.8 million, with U.S. stocks closed.
- Trading in Hyperliquid’s Tesla contract rose from $2.8 million to $47 million in a single hour overnight. It is already the contract’s second-busiest day since launch.
- The contract’s price rose about 5% to roughly $378. Binance’s Tesla contract was still the largest, with $279 million in 24-hour volume against Hyperliquid’s $159 million, according to RootData.
- The contract tracks Tesla’s stock price but is not a tokenized share. It trades around the clock and allows up to 20x leverage.
Traders rushed into Tesla-linked crypto markets overnight after Elon Musk unveiled a flying version of the Roadster, with trading on Hyperliquid jumping while U.S. stock markets were closed.
The surge shows how crypto exchanges that never close are becoming the first place investors react to news about traditional companies.
Musk demonstrated the prototype, which uses SpaceX thruster technology, on Oct. 15, after Tesla · shares closed at $362.44. Hyperliquid’s TSLA perpetual contract rose about 4.9% to roughly $378, and hourly trading volume leapt about 1,580%, from $2.8 million to $47 million. 
It is already the contract’s second-busiest day since listing a year ago, with the daily candle only nine hours old. Binance remained the largest venue, with $279 million in 24-hour volume versus Hyperliquid’s $159 million, according to RootData, but Hyperliquid held the most open interest, at $99 million. Tesla shares were up about 4.5% in premarket trading.
Hyperliquid’s contract, listed through Trade.xyz, is a perpetual future that tracks Tesla’s stock price rather than a tokenized share. It settles in USDC, allows up to 20x leverage and requires no brokerage account. The contract trades around the clock, so it was one of the few ways to bet on Tesla’s price while Nasdaq was closed. Tesla is due to report third-quarter earnings on Oct. 21.

articles.title: Microsoft president warns Trump's immigration crackdown could drive top AI talent abroad
articles.author: Thibault Spirlet
articles.content:
If America wants to win the AI race, sending the world's brightest engineers packing might not be a winning strategy.
That's the warning from Microsoft President Brad Smith, who said the Trump administration's immigration crackdown risks driving the next generation of AI talent away from the United States.
"I think we should all be worried about sending intentionally or inadvertently or otherwise, signals that send the most talented next wave of AI software engineers to other countries rather than the United States," Smith said in an episode of Politico's "The Decoded Podcast" that aired on Thursday.
His comments come after the Trump administration announced last week that it was suspending Microsoft, Adobe, and several other technology companies from a federal program that sponsors foreign workers for permanent residency.
Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program by laying off American employees while hiring lower-paid foreign workers.
Smith, who Business Insider reported was recently put in charge of Microsoft's communications, pushed back against those allegations, saying the administration had presented a misleading picture of Microsoft's hiring practices.
"What was presented as Microsoft replacing 6,000 people who lost their jobs with 9,000 foreigners was frankly completely off base," he said.
Smith said most of the company's visa and green card applications concerned existing employees rather than new hires, adding that Microsoft had hired 9,200 American workers in its last fiscal year.
"That was left out of the narrative," he said.
He also rejected suggestions that Microsoft pays foreign workers less than their American counterparts, saying employees are compensated under the same system regardless of immigration status.
The American dream, on hold
The dispute comes amid growing uncertainty for skilled foreign workers in the US.
As part of our ongoing H-1B Fallout series, Business Insider previously reported that the Trump administration's shifting immigration policies have prompted some international workers to explore opportunities abroad, including in countries like the UK, Germany, and Canada.
An analysis of federal data by Business Insider found that certified H-1B applications fell 10% in the first nine months of fiscal year 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. Applications for data scientists, however, rose 22.5%, highlighting continued demand for specialized AI talent.
On the Politico podcast, Smith cited immigrants' economic contributions as evidence of what America stands to lose.
He said that five of the six technology and science medal recipients recently honored by President Donald Trump had immigrated to the United States.
According to Smith, the companies associated with those five individuals collectively represent more than a quarter of the S&P 500's market value.
Their contributions, he said, benefit not just technology employees but ordinary Americans whose retirement savings and pension funds are invested in those businesses.
"Think about what those five individuals have done for the well being, even the wealth and standard of living, of Americans across the country," Smith said.
"Let's not put that at risk."

articles.title: Surface Laptop Ultra review: a different kind of MacBook Pro
articles.author: Tom Warren
articles.content:
After setting up Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra, I spent five minutes just staring at it. I wasn’t surprised by its MacBook Pro-like design or blown away by its bright display. I was trying to work out what I’d actually do with a $5,900 laptop.
Surface Laptop Ultra review: a different kind of MacBook Pro
A beautiful laptop built for an AI future that hasn’t quite arrived.
This isn’t just any regular Windows laptop. Microsoft has teamed up with Nvidia to build a high-end laptop to showcase Nvidia’s new Arm-based RTX Spark chips. It’s a big moment for Windows on Arm, as these chips can run demanding AI models locally, alongside the latest AAA games and creative apps. The promise is compelling, but the reality of local AI is much messier.
Getting the most out of the Surface Laptop Ultra, especially my top-of-the-line model, requires coding experience or the patience to experiment with models and AI agents until you find something that works. If that sounds like you, Microsoft might have built the Windows laptop you’ve been waiting for. If not, this might not be the MacBook Pro competitor Microsoft was hoping for.
The Good
- Beautiful hardware design
- Magnetic USB-C charging
- Large haptic trackpad
The Bad
- Local AI feels like a beta
- Some bugs with sound and display
- CPU performance is underwhelming
It feels like Microsoft has finally built the hardware to rival Apple’s pro laptops, thanks to an all-aluminum design, large haptic trackpad, and high-end finish. Even the “nightfall” color is just like Apple’s space black.
There are plenty of meaningful differences, though. The 15-inch mini-LED display can run at up to 2,000 nits of peak HDR brightness, at 262 pixels per inch (3270 x 2180); the MacBook Pro peaks at 1,600 nits. That makes it the brightest display Microsoft has ever shipped on a Surface Laptop. Unlike the MacBook Pro, it’s also a 3:2 touchscreen, perfect for writing code, reading text, or editing photos.
The port selection is similar to the MacBook Pro, with one very big change. You get three USB-C ports, a USB-A port, a single HDMI 2.1b port, SD card reader, and headphone jack. Where it really differs is Microsoft’s new Magnetic Connect. It works just like the old Surface Connect, but through the USB-C port on the right-hand side. Just bring the connector close to the port, and it snaps into place. When you’re not charging, that port works just like the rest of the USB-C ports on the laptop.
Magnetic Connect is one of my favorite additions on the Surface Laptop Ultra. I love how you can reverse the magnetic USB-C charging end, attach it to the power brick, and use the regular USB-C connector at the opposite end of the cable to charge the rest of your devices.
The haptic feedback on the large trackpad is also a welcome addition. It works with things like clicks, drags, and window alignment throughout Windows 11, and the tactile feedback triggers in apps like PowerPoint as you drag and align objects or images in a deck, too. It’s subtle enough to make it feel like you’re really moving windows or interfaces around, but I do wish more apps supported it.
Microsoft has included a 1080p front-facing camera above the screen. The quality is fine for video calls, and it supports Windows Hello face authentication and Windows Studio Effects like automatic framing, eye contact, and background blur.
Not all of the Surface Laptop Ultra hardware is impressive, though. I’ve had issues where I’ve unplugged the charger at 100 percent only for Windows to then immediately report 97 percent battery life. Plugging in would put it back to 100 percent and then it would immediately drop back to 97 percent again each time I unplugged.
It seemed weird so I asked Microsoft about the behavior, and it’s designed this way to make a battery last longer. “When it’s plugged in and the battery is full, the device pauses charging rather than constantly topping off, and resumes only once the level drops to 95 percent,” says Microsoft spokesperson Moses Nsereko. “This reduces wear over time. While plugged in, the indicator shows 100 percent to indicate a full charge. When you unplug, it shows the battery’s exact level right away, which may be a few percent lower.”
I’ve run into some issues with the display, too, where either things felt slightly laggy or there was noticeable ghosting. Moving a window around rapidly sometimes left a little trail. Changing power settings from the default “best power efficiency” mode to “best performance” seemed to fix most of the laggy feeling, and the backlight ghosting seems to be less noticeable the longer you run the laptop.
I also heard some loud pops and bangs from the built-in speakers on the Surface Laptop Ultra. They were loud enough to sound like firecrackers, and I thought the battery was about to die before I realized it was just speaker interference. Rebooting the Surface Laptop Ultra solved this one, but it’s happened a couple of times now.
Speaking of rebooting, I’ve noticed that rebooting the Surface Laptop Ultra is surprisingly slow. This seems like something Microsoft could easily fix with an update, though.
Local AI models and agents
The RTX Spark that powers the Surface Laptop Ultra is designed with local AI models and agents in mind. The variant I’ve been testing has a 20-core CPU that was codesigned by Nvidia and MediaTek paired with a 6,144-CUDA-core GPU — roughly comparable to a mobile RTX 5060 — plus 128GB of unified memory and a 1TB Gen 5 SSD. It’s the top-of-the-line model at $5,899, and I think if you’re considering this particular laptop spec then you have a very specific use case in mind. The base version is $2,599, and it comes with an 18-core CPU, 5,120-CUDA -core GPU, and 24GB of unified memory.
Out of the box, Microsoft prompts Laptop Ultra owners to pick an AI agent. You can choose between Hermes, OpenClaw, and Perplexity. I tried out Hermes and OpenClaw over the past week, but I ran into issues getting OpenClaw to work initially. A reinstall fixed a gateway issue, and then I could name my agent and start using it for local AI tasks.
I configured both Hermes and OpenClaw to use the Qwen3.8-27B model, one of the more powerful local AI models. Because it uses the full power of the Surface Laptop Ultra, it will spin up its fans at full throttle and 100 percent GPU for even the most basic of queries. I asked Hermes to resize and convert some photos from PNG to JPG, a task that would take seconds using a PowerToy utility. It took minutes to complete, all while the fans were buzzing away and the laptop was getting hot.
It’s probably my fault for using such a large model for a basic task, but without testing every single local AI model it’s hard to know which one to pick for each task you need. I asked OpenClaw to build me a smart home dashboard, but it spent 30 minutes spinning up the laptop’s fans and calling various tools to eventually produce nothing but an error.
I don’t have a base Surface Laptop Ultra to test, but it’s easy to see that 24GB of unified memory will mean fewer local AI models to choose from.
I struggled to come up with many compelling use cases for the power of these chips for local AI work. A lot of tasks could simply be done far more quickly and without the laptop fans spinning up by using a free cloud model. The power here is really in leaving the agent running at full throttle to build something overnight, or run a task across large datasets that would normally cost a lot of money in cloud tokens.
I did like that I could do things locally, though, without worrying about the privacy aspects of cloud models. I fed Hermes some audio and video files and it went ahead and created a local llama.cpp server to enable audio transcription. It took some fiddling to get it working, but it could certainly save me having to install transcription apps or pay for a cloud service like Otter.
The thing I didn’t like is that these agents are far from user-friendly, and I’m surprised that Microsoft or Nvidia hasn’t developed its own local AI interface that simplifies a lot of this work. I need to spend more time with both Hermes and OpenClaw, but as someone who doesn’t code it’s clear this is all really targeted toward developers and power users.
Gaming and creative tasks
The Surface Laptop Ultra might not be an official gaming laptop, but it’s certainly capable of running far more of the latest games than Apple’s MacBook Pro. Normally I’d be nervous about Windows on Arm and gaming, given the weak GPU on the Qualcomm Snapdragon X series chips. But this is the first time we’ve seen an Arm CPU paired with a stronger Nvidia GPU, and most games run well for a laptop that’s not the size of a gaming one.
Instead of running a bunch of benchmarks at different settings, I decided to try and find the optimal settings that would allow me to play at around 60fps or more in each game. Because this is an RTX GPU, you also get full support for DLSS, Frame Generation, and ray tracing. So you can enable Frame Generation if you want to get to 120fps to match the 120Hz display.
I was able to run Black Myth: Wukong at 70fps on average at native resolution (3270 x 2180) with medium settings and DLSS performance mode enabled. I ran the same medium settings and DLSS performance in Cyberpunk 2077 and averaged 66fps, and Forza Horizon 6 managed an average of 57fps.
Most games will need to run at medium settings and DLSS performance or balanced to get around 60fps, but there are some exceptions where you’ll need to lower settings or resolution. Gears of War: E-Day averaged 40fps on medium settings and DLSS performance, and I only managed to bump this to 48fps on low settings. I also had to move Doom: The Dark Ages to low settings and DLSS performance to hit an average of 60fps.
I’m spoiled by using an RTX 5090 on a 32-inch 4K screen every day with maxed-out game settings, but I didn’t mind the look of medium settings on a 15-inch display. It felt more like dropping down to console settings, and in some games it’s hard to distinguish the texture differences on a smaller display. I’m one of those gamers who prefers to run at 60fps with lower settings rather than max out the settings and have to play at 30fps, though.
While game compatibility is good for most titles, there are some where you’re going to run into emulation issues. Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered was limited to 30fps at 1440p regardless of whether I used low or medium settings. I believe this is because the game is CPU-heavy, so a native Arm port would probably help for this type of game.
There aren’t many native Arm games, though. I tried out the new Arm version of Marvel Rivals, and it averaged 64fps with medium settings and DLSS performance and 75fps with low settings. I think we’ll only see Arm ports where there’s a lot of CPU activity involved that the Prism emulator — which translates CPU instructions from x86 to Arm — can’t handle well enough, because otherwise it’s very capable.
We may see more Arm ports for games that have anti-cheat engines. Anti-cheat engines are a lot more complicated to emulate, so developers have to create Arm-compatible versions. While games like Arc Raiders, Counter-Strike 2, Dota 2, and Fortnite all work out of the box, Nvidia and Microsoft are working with EA, Activision, and Riot Games to get titles like Battlefield, Call of Duty, Valorant, and League of Legends fully supported.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is also a very capable machine for creative and everyday tasks. I managed to export our 4K video test in two minutes and 18 seconds on the Surface Laptop Ultra using Premiere Pro. That’s around a minute behind the top-of-the-line MacBook Pro, but beats the base M5 chip and is around 30 seconds behind the M5 Pro. I did have to create this using Premiere Pro’s own export tool, rather than sending it to Media Encoder like how we usually run this test. There seems to be a bug in the beta Arm version of Media Encoder that prevented it from running the export correctly.
Where the Surface Laptop Ultra really falls behind Apple’s M5 chips is in CPU performance. Single-core and multi-threaded CPU tests like Geekbench or Cinebench show how much weaker the MediaTek CPU is against a $6,999-plus MacBook Pro 16 with an M5 Max or even an M6 Mac Mini. Even some of the GPU tests for Geekbench show the RTX Spark falling behind Apple’s MacBook Pro, and the Puget Bench Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and DaVinci Resolve are all noticeably behind the M5 Max.
I’ve also been testing the battery life of the Surface Laptop Ultra, which seems to be around seven hours if you’re using local AI models and a mix of apps and gaming. If you’re doing less intensive work, it’s averaging out at 10 hours or more. I’ll know more the longer I use the Laptop Ultra, so check back for updated battery impressions.
The Surface Laptop Ultra doesn’t really offer a clear performance advantage over the MacBook Pro outside of some AI workloads like image generation and the ability to run CUDA compute natively. It’s not transformative for the Windows world like the M1 chips were for macOS, largely because Qualcomm already supercharged Windows on Arm with its Snapdragon X series two years ago. That makes it difficult to recommend unless you’re specifically interested in running local AI models, coding, or experimenting with AI agents.
The Surface Laptop Ultra, and Nvidia’s RTX Spark in general, targets developers and power users who want a laptop that can handle those workloads alongside creative apps and the latest games. For that audience, there’s a lot to like. For everyone else, more affordable laptops can handle everyday productivity, creative work, and some light gaming without the hefty price premium.
Microsoft has come closer than ever to building a Windows alternative to the MacBook Pro. The hardware looks and feels great, and Nvidia’s GPU brings CUDA support and decent gaming capabilities to a high-end laptop design. But the Surface Laptop Ultra’s biggest selling point is also its biggest question mark: local AI. It all feels like a work in progress. If you’re ready to experiment with it, this could be a compelling glimpse of where Windows laptops could go next. If you’re not, it’s a lot of money to spend on an experiment.

articles.title: Why education IT teams must protect both human and machine identities
articles.author: Anne Cutler
articles.content:
At the start of every school year, schools, colleges and universities across the UK race to onboard thousands of new students, faculty and staff members, provisioning accounts, issuing credentials and connecting a wave of new devices to institutional networks.
That operational pressure creates opportunities for attackers, and this year, AI is amplifying the threat more than ever. Not only are phishing campaigns more convincing, but a hidden layer of unmanaged machine identities is expanding the cyber attack surface.
VP of Global Communications at Keeper Security.
Attackers are persistent and the education sector remains a top target with many facing cyber attacks weekly. The UK Government’s cyber security breaches survey revealed that 27% of further and higher education institutions reported experiencing a breach or attack at least weekly, compared to 14% of primary schools and 20% of secondary schools.
Navigating the expanded threat window
The education sector is one of the highest targeted industries for ransomware, credential theft and data breaches. For hackers, schools and universities present an appealing combination of high-value data, including student records, financial information and research, alongside underfunded IT departments and an enormous, ever-rotating user base.
The back-to-school season intensifies this pressure. Bulk account creation, mass device enrolment and a surge of third-party application onboarding all happen simultaneously, creating a greater risk of misconfiguration and excessive access rights. The UK Government found that no tier of the education sector had a majority of institutions compliant with all of the government’s Cyber Security 10 Steps.
Just 14% of primary schools, 23% of secondary schools, 33% of further education colleges and 45% of higher education institutions had covered all 10. As thousands of new identities and devices enter this already insecure environment, gaps in security controls can become harder to identify and manage.
AI has made cybersecurity threats significantly more dangerous. The same government survey found phishing to be the main threat identified by institutions that had suffered a breach, and those emails can now precisely mimic communications from student funding offices, IT helpdesks or university leadership, with none of the traditional red flags that once made them easy to spot.

Keeper Security’s research into AI and cybersecurity in education found that 41% of schools have experienced AI-related cyber incidents, including phishing and misinformation, while 90% of education leaders expressed concern about AI-related cybersecurity threats. Yet only one in four respondents felt very confident recognizing AI-enabled threats such as deepfakes or AI-driven phishing.
As AI makes social engineering attacks more convincing, education institutions need to reinforce human awareness with stronger identity and access controls that do not rely on users spotting every malicious message.
The hidden attack surface: non-human identities in EdTech
As students and staff begin the new academic year, IT teams will rightly be focused on securing human accounts, but there is another, much larger population of digital identities that can easily escape attention: Non-Human Identities (NHIs).
NHIs are now embedded throughout modern education environments, from service accounts that synchronize student records with learning platforms to API keys connecting third-party applications, digital textbooks and payment systems.
Machine identities and certificates authenticate everything from campus Wi-Fi and smart boards to lab equipment and security cameras, while cloud workloads automate backups, research pipelines and administrative processes. Similarly, AI agents powering admissions chatbots, helpdesks and grading tools are adding yet another layer of identities and access privileges that institutions need to manage.
These identities are essential to keeping schools and universities running, but they can also create significant security gaps when credentials are rarely rotated, old integration tokens remain active or automated accounts are granted more access than they need.
Unlike employees and students, NHIs are not naturally caught by onboarding and offboarding processes. Without a complete inventory, organizations can struggle to know which identities exist, who owns them and what they can access.
The cybersecurity conversation in education has historically centered on protecting students, teachers and administrators, but the machine identities powering modern EdTech deserve the same scrutiny, because regardless of whether a breach stems from a human or machine, the impact is the same.
Back-to-school is a useful opportunity to review the full identity estate – both human and non-human – remove identities that are no longer required and tighten access for those that remain.
How education IT teams can reduce their risk
For most institutions, the fundamentals of managing humans are manageable. The critical gap is visibility and governance over the NHIs that power modern EdTech, like service accounts, API tokens, machine certificates and AI agents that multiply with every new integration. Security teams should take these steps to help secure NHIs and humans alike.
Enable multi-factor authentication
As the new semester begins, organizations should ensure MFA is enforced across all faculty, staff and student accounts, with new users defaulted into it from the moment they are provisioned. MFA remains a fundamental defense against credential-based attacks.
Audit privileged access
Many accounts give users privileged access beyond what’s necessary for their role. Privileges should be audited for both humans and non-humans. This includes removing access for departed employees and students, retiring expired service accounts and eliminating unnecessary administrative privileges.
Deploy enterprise password managers
Password security remains one of the hardest problems for security teams to solve. Awareness and training can provide students, faculty and staff with the knowledge on how to create strong passwords, but converting that knowledge into practice is difficult because password reuse, written passwords and browser storage remain common. Enterprise password managers remove that gap, enabling users to create and store strong, unique credentials.
Build a non-human identity inventory
You can’t secure what you can’t see. Schools should catalogue every service account, API key, machine certificate, cloud identity and AI agent. Establish ownership and record what each identity can access.
Establish credential rotation policies
It’s important to establish credential rotation policies for machine identities, paying particular attention to AI agents and third-party EdTech integrations added for the new school year. The Canvas learning management system hack, reported in April 2026, affected almost 9,000 educational institutions globally – a reminder that third-party credentials require the same rotation discipline as internal accounts.
Third-party access should be regularly examined and security teams should scrutinize the security of all current and potential partners and suppliers.
Updated training
Security awareness training needs to keep pace with the threat landscape, particularly around phishing, where AI-generated messages may be indistinguishable from legitimate institutional communications. Staff should independently verify unusual requests rather than relying on visual cues alone
Getting ahead of the rush
Back-to-school will always put education IT teams under pressure, but it does not have to create an open window for attackers. As institutions begin the new academic year, security must extend beyond onboarding students and staff to understanding every identity with access to critical systems and data.
By enforcing strong authentication, tightening privileged access, improving credential hygiene and gaining visibility over the growing population of non-human identities, IT teams can significantly reduce their exposure.
Security should be treated as a continuous discipline, not a back-to-school checklist. It is critical that every human and machine identity has the right access, for the right purpose and for only as long as it is needed.

### Key Points
- UK government data shows 27% of higher education institutions experience weekly cyberattacks, significantly higher than the 14% reported by primary schools.
- AI-driven phishing campaigns now mimic official communications from IT helpdesks and student funding offices, making them increasingly difficult for staff and students to identify.
- Non-Human Identities (NHIs), including API keys, service accounts, and AI agents, often lack proper oversight, creating hidden vulnerabilities in modern EdTech environments.
- Only 45% of higher education institutions currently comply with all 10 steps of the UK government’s cyber security guidance.
- Security experts recommend enforcing multi-factor authentication, auditing privileged access, and maintaining a comprehensive inventory of all machine identities to mitigate these risks.

### Why it Matters
The education sector remains a primary target for ransomware and data theft due to its vast stores of personal information and often underfunded IT infrastructure. By failing to secure both human and non-human digital identities, institutions risk significant operational disruption and the compromise of sensitive research and financial data.

articles.title: Bots Used to Be a Threat. Now They’re Your Customers.
articles.author: Andrew Higgins
articles.content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
For the last thirty years, digital marketers have been focused on keeping bots out. The very term “bots” had a negative connotation, and the layers and layers of protection we’ve built are now a liability to brands’ web stacks.
This isn’t because security stopped mattering… It hasn’t. But all of the CAPTCHAs, rate limits, login walls, fingerprinting and internet fortresses we’ve tried to build must be re-examined in the modern context of AI. Brands may be doing themselves a disservice with the default position that automated traffic is hostile until proven otherwise.
My co-founder has been preaching about this for years, and I’ve nodded along for most of them. Only recently have I felt the upside-downness of it, and how much of what we built to protect brands now works against us.
Understanding the scale of the problem
Bots are now 53% of web traffic — that’s the stat everyone repeats on LinkedIn. Although if you double-click, the context is even more important since agents are doing way more than they used to. Often, they don’t just scan sites; they interact and execute workflows, which makes good and bad traffic harder to tell apart.
That is where the problem lies and what we need to solve for — Your defenses can’t tell the difference between someone scraping your catalog nefariously and someone’s assistant trying to buy from it. Same door, same knock. It is hard to distinguish between bots working on behalf of a company, agents working for a consumer, and bad actors (who are still bad actors).
Brands are starting to adopt new strategies
As agents act more and more on behalf of consumers, websites begin to hold a very different spot in the customer journey. A customer tells their assistant: “Find me trail runners, men’s size 10.5, waterproof, under $150, at my door by Saturday.” That agent lands on your site and starts guessing. It reads your page code, infers what your buttons do, and clicks.
Now think about what happens when it doesn’t work or it can’t get proper access. The agent doesn’t email support or try again tomorrow. It moves to a site that was easier to operate and tells your customer it found the shoes there. No cart, no session, no signal anything happened.
That’s the shift marketers should feel in their chest. Site friction used to cost you conversion rate. Now it costs you the consideration set, silently, before a number lands in your analytics.
Instead of the agent reverse-engineering your site, brands need to adopt new protocols and site structures that are helpful, not defensive of bots. The risk is that skipping this means agents may route around you to marketplaces and resellers where the data is easy to get. Your product becomes a row in somebody else’s comparison table. No brand story, no bundle, no reason to pick you over the line below except price and a star.
Bots must be considered a first-class audience when optimizing your website and digital experience. Here are a few things that brands need to consider as they evolve their web experiences for both human consumers & bots.
1. Find out what you’re blocking and make it easier for “good bots” to consume your site
Your bot policy likely got set by a vendor default at some point and often nobody has opened it since. There’s a real chance you’re blocking some of your own demand and calling it protection. 
Example: Plenty of brands still block important buts like ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity use to fetch pages when someone asks a question. If those bots can’t reach your site, you can’t be cited when a shopper asks AI what to buy.
2. Make sure that your site structure is laid out well for agents, and not just well styled
Structure beats styling when it comes to agents. Structuring data such as pricing, availability/inventory, FAQs, sizing, shipping windows, return policy, etc. is incredibly important.
Example: Having Ratings & Reviews data live a well designed carousel or an image, means they don’t exist to agents.
3. Map your customer journey and make sure the actions agents need to take are well articulated
Start by identifying the key things a customer would want an agent to do on your site and optimize specifically for those.
Example: A footwear brand would want to make sure agents can easily navigate to buy their products, read reviews, and compare to their main competitors. Given these are all steps in journey an agent is likely to take on behalf of a shopper, brands must re-engineer parts of their website to make these steps seamless not just for human shoppers but agents too.
4. Revamp your analytics stack
Often an agent visits your site and reports back to the consumer on a different surface than your website. Ultimately, what matters is whether you showed up, got cited, and got picked within the AI Search interaction between AI and your customer. But it also means your web analytics are not a trustworthy source of truth when agents are the ones visiting it, and then taking the data and experience onto new surfaces not mapped by your web analytics.
Example: Your organic search traffic may have dropped 35% over the past few quarters, but that does not necessarily mean you have gotten 35% less organic impressions. It’s likely that the impressions have just moved from your website (between you and your shopper), and are now taking place across large language models (between an agent and your shopper). For many brands this means a new set of metrics and analytics are required to understand how bots and AI are changing organic discovery. 
Conclusion
None of this means the last thirty years were a mistake. The gates were correct for the internet we had. They’re just pointed at the wrong thing now.
It’s also important to acknowledge that evolving for an agentic internet isn’t just an SEO tweak or checklist to work through. It’s architectural, and marketing owns more of it than marketing expects. Nobody from security is going to walk into your Monday standup and tell you the bot rules are costing you customers.
For the last thirty years, digital marketers have been focused on keeping bots out. The very term “bots” had a negative connotation, and the layers and layers of protection we’ve built are now a liability to brands’ web stacks.
This isn’t because security stopped mattering… It hasn’t. But all of the CAPTCHAs, rate limits, login walls, fingerprinting and internet fortresses we’ve tried to build must be re-examined in the modern context of AI. Brands may be doing themselves a disservice with the default position that automated traffic is hostile until proven otherwise.
My co-founder has been preaching about this for years, and I’ve nodded along for most of them. Only recently have I felt the upside-downness of it, and how much of what we built to protect brands now works against us.
