Digital marketers must shift from blocking automated traffic to optimizing websites for AI agents, as restrictive security measures now risk excluding brands from modern consumer discovery and purchasing.

### Key Points
- Bots currently account for 53% of all web traffic, necessitating a shift in how brands manage automated interactions.
- Overly restrictive security measures like CAPTCHAs and login walls can prevent AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude from indexing essential product information.
- Brands should prioritize structured data for pricing, inventory, and shipping to ensure AI agents can accurately interpret and present their offerings.
- Traditional web analytics may no longer reflect true organic discovery, as consumer interactions increasingly occur within AI-driven search interfaces rather than on brand websites.
- Companies must re-engineer site architectures to treat "good bots" as a primary audience to avoid being bypassed by marketplaces and resellers.

### Why it Matters
As AI agents increasingly act on behalf of consumers to research and purchase products, websites that block these tools risk losing visibility and sales. Brands that fail to adapt their digital infrastructure may find themselves excluded from the consideration set, effectively ceding their market presence to competitors with more accessible data.

articles.title: I've spent over $3,000 on ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, and only one was worth the money
articles.author: Mahnoor Faisal
articles.content:
Something I remember particularly well about the early days of generative AI is how quickly people developed an aversion to the idea of paying for yet another subscription. I could understand why! We were already paying monthly for everything from streaming services to cloud storage, and suddenly, using a chatbot just to draft a quick email or (unfortunately) write an essay was going to cost another $20 a month.
In fact, when ChatGPT Plus first launched in February 2023, Reddit was filled with people questioning whether a chatbot could possibly be worth that much. Fast forward a few years, and I've somehow managed to spend over $3,000 on subscriptions to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini alone.
After spending that much money, I've come to realize that paying for an AI subscription isn't necessarily a waste of money. Paying for the wrong one, however, absolutely can be! So, here's the only one I'd happily continue paying for...
ChatGPT Plus is the easiest subscription to justify
OpenAI has finally won me over
If you'd told me six months ago that I'd be recommending a $20 ChatGPT Plus subscription over a $100 Claude Max subscription, I'd have looked you right in the eyes and laughed. However, over the last few weeks, ChatGPT has undeniably jumped to the very top of my list, and it's not even a particularly close competition anymore.
For starters, OpenAI's models have gotten significantly better. I've noticed the difference most when using Codex and Claude Code side by side, especially when giving both tools the exact same task. There was a time when Claude Code would consistently deliver better results, particularly when it came to building polished interfaces and figuring out what I wanted without needing me to spell out every little detail. Lately, though, the tables have turned. Codex has been doing a much better job of understanding my intentions, making sensible decisions on its own, and delivering finished products that actually feel finished.
Even when I preferred Claude for coding, I was always vocal about how ChatGPT still excelled as a general-purpose AI assistant. Whether I needed help researching a topic, understanding a complicated concept, brainstorming ideas, or simply figuring something out, ChatGPT was almost always the first tool I'd turn to. Now that Codex has caught up with, and in some cases surpassed, Claude Code in my own testing, I'm finding fewer and fewer reasons to pay for a separate Claude subscription.
The biggest reason, though, is the limits. Claude frankly has absurd usage limits, and I manage to hit my weekly limit just three days into the week! On the contrary, I can get through an entire week of using Codex on my $20 ChatGPT Plus subscription without running into nearly as many restrictions. Considering I was paying five times as much for Claude Max, it's becoming increasingly difficult to justify spending that kind of money when the cheaper alternative lets me get more work done.
Claude has lost the edge it once had
Oh, how the tables have turned
While I've already addressed most of the reasons I don't prefer Claude nearly as much as I used to, I think the biggest one is that it no longer has the unique edge that once made it so easy to recommend. It's not necessarily that Claude has gotten significantly worse. Rather, competing LLMs have caught up with, and in some cases surpassed, the things Claude used to do better than everyone else. And when that happens, all the little frustrations you've been willing to overlook suddenly become a lot harder to ignore.
I also feel like Anthropic has sort of slowed down in the last few months. I've always praised the company for staying ahead of the curve and introducing features that genuinely change how people use AI, rather than simply chasing whatever its competitors are doing. Lately, though, it feels like OpenAI has been moving at a much faster pace, rolling out new features and improvements that give me more reasons to keep coming back. That's not to say Claude has stopped improving, but for the first time in a long while, I find myself getting more excited about what OpenAI is doing than what Anthropic has up its sleeve.
Unfortunately, it's not just the pace of innovation that's been bothering me. A couple of months ago, I wrote an entire article about how exhausting Claude had become to use, particularly for research. Despite using its most capable model at the highest effort setting, I kept finding that Claude would rush through research tasks, overlook useful sources, or answer questions without even bothering to search the web.
In one experiment, I gave Claude and ChatGPT the exact same research question. Claude spent roughly a minute and a half putting together its answer, while ChatGPT spent around 12 minutes digging into the topic. The difference in the quality and depth of their responses was enough to make me question what I was paying so much more for.
Then there's the fact that Claude has occasionally taken it upon itself to decide how I should use my remaining allowance. I've had Claude Code discourage me from continuing a task because I was approaching my usage limit, even though I was perfectly happy to use whatever I had left. I understand warning users before they run out, but I don't think a tool I'm paying $100 a month for should be making that decision for me.
None of this means Claude is a bad AI assistant. Far from it! There are still things I prefer about Claude, and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend trying it. But recommending Claude and recommending a paid Claude subscription are two very different things. With the competition getting better and the frustrations piling up, I just don't see enough reasons to keep paying for Claude Max anymore.
Gemini is the weakest reason to pay for Google AI Pro
Everything but the chatbot makes it worthwhile
Google AI Pro is a slightly different story. Unlike ChatGPT Plus and Claude Pro, where the main selling point is access to better AI models and higher usage limits, Google's subscription comes bundled with a bunch of other perks that make it surprisingly easy to justify.
For instance, I use NotebookLM practically every day for studying, and I genuinely wouldn't hesitate to pay $20 a month for its premium features alone. The higher limits are incredibly useful, especially when I'm working with multiple lectures, readings, and presentations. So, the fact that Google AI Pro includes an upgraded NotebookLM experience alongside 5TB of cloud storage, Gemini integrations across Google's productivity apps, and access to other tools like Flow and Antigravity makes it a pretty compelling package.
There's even YouTube Premium Lite included in select countries, which is a nice bonus if you're someone who spends a ridiculous amount of time watching YouTube. And if you already rely heavily on Gmail, Google Docs, and Drive, I can absolutely see Google AI Pro being the subscription that makes the most financial sense for you.
The problem, at least for me, is Gemini itself. While Google's models have certainly improved, I still find myself turning to ChatGPT or Claude for most of the things I'd normally use a general-purpose AI assistant for. Whether it's brainstorming ideas, researching something, or tackling a complicated task, Gemini rarely ends up being my first choice.
In every comparison where I've pitted Codex, Claude Code, and Antigravity against each other, Antigravity has, without fail, been the one that disappointed me the most. It's not necessarily that it can't get the job done, but the results often feel far less polished than what its competitors deliver. I've had instances where Antigravity declared a project finished despite leaving out features I'd explicitly requested, and others where I had to step in to fix problems that ideally should've been caught during testing.
That's ultimately why I find Google AI Pro a little difficult to recommend purely for Gemini. The subscription itself offers tremendous value, particularly if you're already invested in Google's ecosystem, but I don't think the chatbot or coding experience alone is compelling enough to make me choose it over ChatGPT Plus.
So, all that to say, the subscription I can most easily recommend right now is ChatGPT Plus. Claude would be my next pick if you're looking for an AI assistant primarily for writing or coding, though I'd think twice before splurging on its more expensive tiers. I'd only recommend Google AI Pro if the AI itself isn't your main reason for subscribing, and you're more interested in perks like NotebookLM, cloud storage, and integrations with Google's other services.
articles.summary:
OpenAI’s ChatGPT Plus has emerged as the most justifiable AI subscription, outperforming competitors like Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini in coding capabilities, research depth, and overall usage value.

### Key Points

- Anthropic’s Claude Max subscription is criticized for high costs, restrictive usage caps, and inconsistent research quality compared to OpenAI’s models.

- The author reports spending over $3,000 on AI subscriptions, concluding that ChatGPT Plus offers the best balance of utility and price.
- Competitive pressure has forced rapid innovation, with OpenAI currently outpacing Anthropic in feature rollouts and model reliability.

### Why it Matters
Choosing the right AI subscription is increasingly important as monthly costs for these tools accumulate for professional and personal users. Evaluating these services based on actual performance and usage limits helps consumers avoid paying for redundant or underperforming software in a rapidly evolving market.

articles.title: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost
articles.author: Radhika Rajkumar
articles.content:
ZDNET’s key takeaways
- AI-related job losses impact local community economics.
- The CAIS tracker puts these losses in dollars and cents.
- Understanding how AI will change the economy still involves guesswork.
Fears of how AI will impact the economy and job availability are running rampant after a few years of steady layoffs at major companies. Much of that fear can be attributed to labs and CEOs juicing their own relevance, but some job cuts have been explicitly tied to AI’s rapid acceleration.
The Center for AI Safety (CAIS) maintains a tracker that keeps tabs on how these changes are impacting family wages.
Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires
More from ZDNET
The Wage Loss Dashboard includes a map of where layoffs have occurred since January 2026 (it was just updated this month to include September data) and a drop-down that shows data for the entire country or an individual state. As of now, the dashboard finds just over 117,000 job cuts attributed to AI nationally this year — $8.5 billion in estimated annual wage losses.
The Wage Loss Dashboard multiplies the number of AI-attributed job cuts by the average annual salary to estimate annual wage loss. According to the dashboard, wage estimates “begin to show what those cuts can mean for households and local economies.”
The dashboard also displays the estimated average wage loss per person based on that layoff data, presented relative to everyday expenses, like a tank of gas. For the country as a whole, it’s $25 per person per year. Not much, but the numbers shift by state: In California, for example, it’s $56. That’s thanks to a much higher concentration of job cuts (just over 27,000 layoffs attributed to AI). Alaska, on the other hand, claims only 138 job losses ($14 per person).
Those aren’t the exact numbers of people laid off for AI in California and Alaska this year, however. As CAIS explains, “The dashboard estimates AI-attributed cuts for each state, converts them to estimated annual wage loss, then divides by state population to estimate the average loss per person. State estimates are not observed AI layoffs. We apply each month’s national share of cuts citing AI to that state’s announced job cuts.”
From layoffs to dollars and cents
The dashboard uses a few sources of data: monthly reporting from Challenger, Gray, and Christmas, which compiles layoff announcements from across the US by state as well as national job cuts credited to AI, and data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics on every state’s annual mean wage. CAIS also refers to population estimates from the US Census Bureau.
Also: 3 ways AI can help you ace your next job interview
In 2025, the Challenger, Gray, and Christmas reports identified over 54,000 job cuts that companies publicly linked to AI. That translates to one in 20 layoffs from last year. But tracking job losses alone is a more abstract metric than what those layoffs mean in monetary terms to the people experiencing them.
“There has been significant news coverage of job loss from AI, but it can be hard to quantify how these cuts affect the average person’s finances,” CAIS wrote of the project. “This dashboard aims to help illuminate the monetary costs of AI on American families and communities.”
As CAIS points out, the impact of layoffs shows up in ripples across grocery stores, small businesses, rent, and other local costs.
“One person’s layoff means less income for every business they support. Multiply that effect across thousands of workers in multiple industries, and you start to see the real economic weight of AI displacement,” the researchers behind the project wrote. “In addition, AI-attributed job cuts aren’t spread evenly. States with large tech and media sectors are experiencing greater impact.”
A few caveats: CAIS noted that this dashboard doesn’t include “jobs created by AI, productivity gains, re-employment, or secondary economic effects.” That’s partly because experts don’t have a consensus on whether or how much AI will stimulate the economy or outpace job displacement. AI-attributed layoffs are themselves murky: The data here are job cuts companies themselves said were tied to AI. Without a single definition for what that means or complete transparency from companies, it’s not always 100% provable that a layoff was the direct result of obsolescence or replacement spurred by AI.
Also: Companies embracing AI the most are hiring more people
“We don’t require an executive to say ‘we replaced a team with AI.’ This is a moderate standard, deliberately: it captures the broad pattern of AI-justified workforce reductions while excluding clearly unrelated cuts,” the Alliance for Secure AI wrote of its methodology.
Other trackers like Jobloss.ai, which is run by the Alliance for Secure AI, also catalog job loss data by company, date, and how explicitly companies cited AI around those layoffs. Because of how amorphous these data can be to track, Jobloss.ai only logs layoffs that meet certain criteria: at least 100 jobs in one fell swoop, accompanied by some mention of AI (or proxy terms, like “automation” and “productivity”).
The dashboard aims to make the data we do have more accessible — not to shame any particular industry or company for its AI adoption choices.
“AI is a technology being adopted by companies for many reasons,” CAIS wrote. “Our goal is to make the costs of that adoption visible, so workers, communities, and policymakers can respond with real information instead of guesses.”
Automating remote labor
The Wage Loss Dashboard also includes a section on how well AI is completing remote freelance tasks. Using data from the Remote Labor Index (RLI) benchmark CAIS co-developed, which tests agents on real-world freelance tasks like web development and video production, CAIS shows how quickly agents are evolving.
“When RLI launched, the best AI agent completed just 2.5% of projects at professional quality. Eight months later, that number has risen to 15.8%,” researchers wrote. As of now, AI can fully automate almost 16% of remote tasks, a percentage that’s doubling every 3.7 months. Claude Fable 5 comes in on top, followed by OpenAI’s GPT-5.5.
But that doesn’t mean AI is gobbling up those projects from human freelancers. RLI measures what AI models are capable of doing, not what they’re actively taking on. That said, CAIS maintains alarm about what it sees as a trend: the convergence of AI-attributed job cuts with increasingly work-capable agents.
While legislation can’t explicitly prevent companies from opting for AI systems over hiring humans in certain cases, recent laws in a few states, including the tech-sector-heavy state of California, aim to make sure firing and other disciplinary decisions aren’t completely automated by AI systems.

- The dashboard tracks over 117,000 job cuts explicitly attributed to AI by companies since January 2026.
- California faces the highest economic impact, with an estimated $56 in annual wage loss per person due to a high concentration of tech-sector layoffs.

- The Remote Labor Index shows AI agents can now complete 15.8% of professional freelance tasks, a figure that is doubling every 3.7 months.
- The tracker excludes potential economic benefits like job creation or productivity gains, focusing solely on the monetary impact of workforce displacement.

### Why it Matters
Quantifying the financial impact of AI-related layoffs helps policymakers and communities move beyond speculation to understand the tangible economic consequences of automation. By visualizing these losses, the dashboard highlights how AI adoption creates uneven regional impacts that ripple through local businesses and household stability.

articles.title: Future of Marketing Briefing: The holdcos long, awkward courtship of the C-suite
articles.author: Seb Joseph
articles.content:
Publicis Groupe CEO Arthur Sadoun said this week that he’s pitching directly to CEOs, and the industry hasn’t stopped chewing it on since.
Some of the messages landing in Digiday’s inbox have him down as a leader in the fullest sense. Plenty of others aren’t buying it. How many chief executives, the doubters ask, decide their business needs transforming and make the first call to an ad holding company? A few go further and read the whole thing as bravado papering over a trail of pitches that went nowhere. Strip out the cheerleading and the snark, and what’s left is an identity crisis holdcos have been struck in for the best part of two decades.
It started around 2008. Clients cut ad budgets the moment the economy wobbled, and the holdcos, badly exposed, went looking for a way into the boardroom. Some managed it. Sir Martin Sorreil made his name at WPP partly on his access to chief executives, and Mark Read kept a smaller version of that going after him. Sorrell’s great rival, Maurice Levy, worked edge same circuit for Publicis long before handing the job to Sadoun. Over at Omnicom, John Wren pulled the same trick, which goes some way to explaining how the group has held on to the likes of Apple and McDonald’s for so long. Still, those relationships tended to grow out of the CMO-holdco tie rather than any standing the holdcos had earned with the rest of the C-suite.
Publicis, according to Sadoun, has found its way in. CEOs, he said, are “increasingly” involved in what the business does, mostly because they’re passionate about AI and need to understand it well enough to make the right calls. It doesn’t take much to work out who he has in mind for the tutoring.
And why not? Few CMOs carry much weight with the rest of the C-suite, and most don’t last in the job long enough for an agency relationship to outlive the retainer. So the holdcos hedged. They spent years buying data companies and consulting shops to prove marketing could move the numbers a finance chief watches, and occasionally to catch the CEOs eye along the way. It only ever half worked. When a chief executive goes looking for outside counsel, the shortlist still tends to start with Accenture and Deloitte, whose boardroom relationships go back decades.
That’s a completely different way of working for agencies. Consultancies are built to play the long game and their staff learn early that helping a client’s people get ahead, even with no fee attached, is how the bigger work eventually lands. Agencies grew up selling to a single buyer in the CMO, one brief at a time. For most of them, the reward for winning a pitch has been the chance to defend it at the next one. Unpicking the kind of loyalty a consultancy has spent decades building with a CEO will take holdcos a lot longer than a good AI pitch.
“Agencies don’t typically have meaningful access to that level of the clients they work with. In packaged goods, they do, luxury is the same – because they are a pretty material part of the business,” said Brian Wieser, media analyst and author of the Madison and Wall newsletter. “What has struck me when I’ve seen it in the wild, is that it’s like a big deal for a an agency CEO to get to meet the CEO of a financial services company or an auto company where advertising and marketing is like a low single digit percentage of total activities.”
Get that meeting, though, and it can pay off handsomely. Sadoun said this week that Publicis Sapient helped land two of the year’s biggest accounts without a pitch. If CEOs can make reviews disappear, they’re the closest thing to a cheat code the agency business has seen in years. The theory is that a holdco gets through the technology door and the media and creative work follows. Getting that to compound is another matter. Sapient is the part of Publicis that’s shrinking — outside of the U.S. at least — down mid-single digits in the second quarter and still slipping slightly in the third. Transformation work is lumpy and can stall the moment clients get nervous, as delayed programs in the Gulf showed this year. The holdcos have also bled the senior people needed to hold the boardroom relationships together, sometimes by design and sometimes by accident.
Then there’s the risk of getting exactly what they asked for. CEOs ask awkward questions for a living, and the holdco model has plenty worth asking about: data charges, tech fees folded into bundled deals and principal media, where the holdco buys inventory itself and sells it on at a margin clients don’t always see.
“All of that stuff doesn’t hold enough water for the rest of the C-suite,” said Steve Boehler, who runs consultancy Mercer Island Group. Pull those executives into the relationship and the holdocs will have “really smart people trying to look under the hood,” he said, who may be unable to see what they’re really buying.”
None of this means holdco bosses are wrong to covet CEOs. Boehler sees the push as part of a wider shift in what marketing covers, closer to the old four Ps of product, price, pace and promotion than to the advertising the agencies were built around. The holdco now has “at least on paper,” the capability to address the needs that “touch multiple people in that C-suite,” he said. That spreads the buying decision across more desks. The silos inside most big companies “have considerable power and influence,” said Boehler, so the CEO and CFO end up with a say in the pitches that used to sit with CMO, whether they show up in the room or not. He expects considerably more to happen before any of it sticks. The ambition itself, he said, is “a real intention” of the holdcos.
When it does stick, the marketers who used to own the relationship can find themselves on the outside of it. A senior marketer at one advertiser described a holdco deal that has run for several years with an agency the team likes. The trouble is that the holdco’s chief client officer has grown closer to the company’s C-suite. When the internal media buying team raises a complaint now, it struggles to get a hearing, because it’s no longer the agency’s main sponsor inside the business.
Two decades spent trying to get past the CMO and the holdcos may find the CMO was the one relationship they couldn’t afford to lose.
Billion Dollar Boy goes shopping
Billion Dollar Boy has bought something. The social marketing agency spent a decade building its business organically, so its acquisition of Creator Authority, a B2B creator marketing specialist with LinkedIn accreditation, marks a charge in habit. The deal also gives BDB more presence in LA and Austin. Thomas Walters, the agency’s chief innovation officer, said the firm spotted B2B marketing heating up 18 months ago and hinted that more deals are coming. The conversation that follows has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Why B2B, and why now?
Walters: We identified about 18 months ago that B2B marketing was heating up. Its shown promise for a ling time but hasn;t had the same rigor or professionalization, apart from specialists like Creator Authority. Spend is increasing and marketers are seeing very high ROI for B2B brands, even more markedly than B2C because it’s newer. Creator Authority was growing very quickly and dealing with some of the growing pains we went through as a younger business. We can support them through that. We’re very confident that with the combination of our global platform and Creator Authority’s special relationships, and LinkedIn accreditation,-that we can make a really serious mark in professionalizing and advancing the B2B creator marketing industry as a whole.
How much do the two client bases overlap?
Walters: The client mix is different but there’s crossover. Microsoft, for example, is a client we share. Some businesses sell to other businesses, some sell directly to consumers and some do both. CMOs already work with a proliferation of agencies. Where a client has a B2B and B2C audience we can now offer a combined solution, which saves them managing different partners.
Is this the start of more acquisitions?
Walters: Historically we’ve built things organically, whether that’s investing in creative tech or building direct access to creators. This is our first acquisition. Our long-term plan has strategic moves on it that we’re planning to make and the two approaches compound. As scopes get bigger and capability needs get wider we want to have solutions in market.
Are the briefs changing as a result?
Walters: We’re seeing a creator way of thinking applied to more channels and more parts of the funnel than ever before. Creator content is supporting SEO and now AEO. Creators are being integrated intro branded entertainment and brand films. CMOs want partners that can work across that mix and we’ve been building against those changes for some time, from evolving Billion Dollar Boy into a social agency to creating our production arm about five years ago.
Does calling a BDB a creator agency pigeonhole it?
Walters: Our mission is to transform how brands grow in a creator world. Billion Dollar Boy is a social agency with a creator instinct. We’ve delivered broad social copes for many years and creator fluency has always been in our DNA. In 2026 we;re in what we call social 3.0 where creators are the lifeblood of social media. If brands don;t understand that their advertising won;t engage audiences or drive impact. Many others in the social space are still operating with a social 2.0 mindset.
What we’ve heard
“So more and more we have a region manager and we will ask them to focus on cross-fertilization, on the integration of creative and media. And I would say the ambition in terms of new biz is really attracting this new integrated client that gives to Havas all the assignments from media to production including creativity, data, PR or event.”
— François Laroze, cfo and chief operating officer at Havas on the holdco’s Q3 earnings call earlier this week
Numbers to know
50.1%: Percentage of U.S. generative AI users that will use Google AI Mode over every other AI tool in 2030.
34%: Percentage of ad impressions on Instagram that came from Reels in Q3 2026.
$250 million: The estimated cost for Spotify’s latest multiyear licensing agreement with Joe Rogan.
$3.7 billion: eMarketer’s forecast for Netflix’s U.S. ad revenues in 2027
What we’re reading
YouTube briefly tested a “Channel Search” tab that let a handful of brand channels see opted-in creators’ audience analytics right inside YouTube Studio, to help with sponsorship scouting. YouTube says it’s strictly for brands, not a way for creators to snoop on rivals, per Tube Filter.
Meta has banned ads from ByteDance and any campaigns linking to TikTok across the U.S. and six other markets, calling it normal practice to refuse a competitor’s promotion, according to Bloomberg. It’s the latest escalation in a feud sharpened by Meta’s $18 billion child-safety settlement, which it’s been pressuring TikTok to match.
Nine months after TikTok’s U.S. spin-off closed, employees say little has changed. Staff still collaborate closely with the global company on ByteDance-built tools raising doubts about how real the separation is. With Washington now focused more on child safety than China, those questions have been postponed rather than answered, per Politico.
TikTok CEO Shou Chew and Microsoft’s Judson Althoff both said in Singapore that AI hype has run ahead of what the technology can actually do, noting humans still beat it in key areas and that cybersecurity is the more pressing risk, according to Quartz.
What we’ve covered
PepsiCo CEO Ramon Laguarta used an investor call to champion moving its roughly $1.9 billion global media account from Omnicom to Publicis without a review. He framed it as a data capability rather than an agency relationship, and signalled more marketing investment to revive flagging North American values.
Dentsu wants branded entertainment to be a core budget line rather than an innovation side project, and its backing that by investing in productions like Angry Birds 3 so clients get first dibs on integrations. Cheaper creator-led formats like microdramas have made the pitch much easier to land.
Ikea’s CMO Vincenzo Riili argues that because LLMs draw on everything written about a company, from ads to annual reports, a consistent brand matters more than ever. AI should distribute a brand, not create it, and brands with muddled propositions will suffer when models can’t tell what they stand for.
Universities such as Arizona State, Stanford and Syracuse are launching creator economy degrees, courses and research centres as the industry matures. The focus isn’t only on training on-camera talent, but also the strategists, marketers and operators behind them.
Ruggable is shaking up its marketing stack, pulling dollars our of Meta and into ShopMy creators ahead of a potential IPO.
Guitar brand Fender and amp-maker Marshall both recently launched content series aimed, in part, at improving their visibility in AI search answers. It’s part of a greater pattern.

Publicis Groupe CEO Arthur Sadoun is shifting the agency’s strategy to pitch directly to corporate CEOs, aiming to bypass traditional marketing departments to secure long-term, high-value business partnerships.

### Key Points

### Why it Matters
This shift reflects a broader industry attempt to move marketing from a siloed expense to a core business driver integrated into the C-suite's strategic agenda. If successful, this approach could redefine agency-client relationships, though it risks undermining the essential partnerships agencies have historically maintained with chief marketing officers.

articles.title: Silent Hill And Metal Gear Publisher Konami Does ‘Not Believe The Market Will Shift Significantly’ Because Of AI
articles.author: Alicia Haddick
articles.content:
The question of AI’s impact on their own development practices and the external use of the technology by people infringing on copyrighted material are becoming major topics of concern for many game studios. With Konami releasing its financial statement today, the company used the opportunity to provide its thoughts on the topic.
It’s possible that investor excitement for the technology would make the company feel obligated to address the seismic shifts the industry is facing due to AI, as well as any potential use cases it may have for Konami itself, in its latest the financial report. Notably, the statement focuses on the idea that, no matter the advancements in AI or its capabilities, certain things integral to game development can’t be replaced by technology.
“Generally, it’s thought that AI will allow anyone to easily make games, thus lowering the barrier to entry,” says Hideki Hayakawa, representative director and president at Konami Digital Entertainment. “However, I do not believe the market will shift significantly. Barriers to entry have already been lowered by the growth of general-purpose game engines and the growth of user-generated content in games. Also, even if using AI leads to greater efficiency, I believe the most important factor in developing interesting and innovative games is people, specifically creators. Not only that, creators form ‘teams’ to develop games, and within that, people from diverse backgrounds exchange and bring together ideas to create never-before-seen new games that expand the potential of gaming. This kind of interaction cannot be replaced easily.”
While this doesn’t entirely rule out the company using AI, as the report notes at the same time that the technology presents a “notable opportunity” and could support developers in some ways, Konami remains cautious in researching it while slowly providing guidance to its teams on guardrails and protocols for whether it is to be used. The statement also mirrors that of other studios like Sega, though Konami emphasizes the idea of players and developers coming together in order to have the most fun with a gaming experience, which an AI experience catered solely to the person making it, no matter its quality, cannot offer.
This emphasis on user-generated content may simply be because the studio is currently developing its own alternative to Roblox with Wai Wai World Craft. In any case, it’s notable to see the studio stepping away from a full embrace of the technology.
articles.summary:
Konami president Hideki Hayakawa stated that while artificial intelligence offers development efficiencies, the company believes human creators remain essential for producing innovative and meaningful gaming experiences.

### Key Points
- Konami president Hideki Hayakawa emphasized that human collaboration and diverse team perspectives are irreplaceable in the game development process.
- The company acknowledged that AI presents notable opportunities for efficiency but remains cautious regarding its implementation across development teams.
- Konami is currently establishing internal guardrails and protocols to manage the use of AI technology within its studios.
- The studio is developing a user-generated content platform titled Wai Wai World Craft, which serves as a competitor to Roblox.
- Management believes that existing game engines and user-generated content have already lowered industry barriers more significantly than current AI advancements.

### Why it Matters
This stance highlights a growing trend among major game studios to prioritize human-led creativity over full automation in software development. By resisting a total shift toward AI, Konami aims to preserve the collaborative team dynamics that define its unique gaming experiences.

articles.title: Developers Question Scope of Potential Apple Antitrust Settlement
articles.author: Hartley Charlton
articles.content:
Developers are questioning whether a settlement of the U.S. government's antitrust case against Apple would meaningfully loosen the company's control over the iPhone, according to The Information.
The report highlights PayPal and Epic Games among the companies that have raised concerns with the Department of Justice (DOJ). Officials have reportedly indicated that they favor a negotiated resolution and have asked developers to suggest improvements to how the iPhone works with other companies' products.
These discussions largely center on interoperability, including access for competing accessories and payment services. The concern among developers and antitrust lawyers cited in the report is how much Apple would actually have to change. Rival smartwatches, for example, lack much of the integration available to the Apple Watch, while competing payment apps reportedly still face disadvantages despite gaining access to near-field communication (NFC) technology for contactless payments.
When the DOJ filed its lawsuit in March 2024, it alleged that restrictions affecting messaging, digital wallets, smartwatches, cloud gaming, and multipurpose apps helped Apple unlawfully protect its smartphone monopoly. Apple rejected these allegations and argued that the government's proposed intervention would threaten its ability to design integrated products.
Some of the capabilities at issue have changed since the lawsuit began. Apple added Rich Communication Services (RCS) support to Messages with iOS 18, improving communication with Android phones. It also expanded access to the iPhone's NFC capabilities for third-party contactless transactions starting with iOS 18.1.
According to The Information, Apple offered interoperability concessions during an earlier attempt to avert the lawsuit. The company could still resist the broader changes developers want, leaving the current negotiations without an agreement. Proton said it doubted Apple would accept terms developers would regard as satisfactory.
Note: This discussion thread is located in our Political News forum with special rules.
articles.summary:
Developers and industry stakeholders are questioning whether a potential settlement between the U.S. Department of Justice and Apple will effectively reduce the company's restrictive control over iPhone ecosystems.

### Key Points
- The Department of Justice is currently exploring a negotiated settlement regarding its March 2024 antitrust lawsuit against Apple.
- Companies including Epic Games and PayPal have expressed skepticism that a settlement will sufficiently address Apple's restrictive interoperability policies.
- Discussions focus on expanding third-party access to iPhone hardware features, specifically NFC payment systems and smartwatch integration.
- Apple recently introduced iOS updates providing RCS messaging support and broader NFC access, though critics argue these changes remain insufficient.
- Apple maintains that government intervention threatens its ability to design integrated, secure products for its users.

### Why it Matters
A settlement could set a significant legal precedent for how dominant tech platforms manage third-party access to their proprietary hardware and software ecosystems. If the government accepts limited concessions, it may fail to resolve long-standing competition concerns regarding digital wallets, messaging, and wearable device integration.

articles.title: How Israeli firm’s ‘zero-click’ malware attack poses global security risk
articles.author: Federica Marsi
articles.content:
Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found. You are not even required to “click” on anything.
An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims.
In June 2025, 45 devices used by Al Jazeera staff – including several who reported on sensitive subjects – were targeted with spyware which installed itself without the need to open or download any files.
An investigation by the Canada-based academic research unit Citizen Lab, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, discovered that the Israeli company Candiru was behind the attacks.
Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat. “We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera.
“This is the next level, because people are being microtargeted,” he said. “This is the point we’ve come to when it comes to surveillance.”
How ‘zero-click’ malware works
Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed.
Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners.
Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru. The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists, journalists and political activists across 10 countries.
Al Jazeera Media Network has condemned the targeting of its staff members’ devices and called for those responsible to be held accountable.
Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance. “Executing code inside the browser does not automatically give an attacker full control over the computer,” Willems told Al Jazeera.
“To escape the browser’s isolated environment – the ‘sandbox’ – the attacker may need a second vulnerability,” Willems said, adding that an advanced spyware operation can combine several vulnerabilities.
“The attacker attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security boundaries. This is precisely what makes this type of attack so dangerous,” the analyst said.
Once the device is infected, the malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials.
It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms. To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time.
Advertising: A new global security threat?
Analysts say Citizen Lab’s findings point to the escalation of an existing threat, which expands the scale and reach of traditional cyberattacks and makes them much harder to detect.
While “zero-click” attacks are not completely new, the findings outline a new technique through which online advertisements are used as a route to infection.
Stephen O’Shaughnessy, a lecturer in cybersecurity at the TU Dublin Blanchardstown campus in Ireland, explained that when a user opens a website or app, an automated auction sells the advertisement space in a fraction of a second. That auction shares data about the victim, including the device ID, IP address, rough location and the app or site they are on.
“Discover-Tech posed as an ordinary advertiser, used that data to find their target and win the auction for that person’s screen,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera. “Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.”
“Because no message or link is involved, there is almost nothing for the victim to notice,” he added.
Discover-Tech appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served advertisements via major networks such as Google, Yandex and Beeswax.
In its report, Citizen Lab said this illustrates the structural flaws in the online advertising system, which essentially failed to detect or prevent the abuse.
Discover-Tech advertisements have popped up on devices used by personnel in national-security-sensitive networks around the world, including those of various ministries of defence, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organisations and media outlets, Citizen Lab found.
The research unit said these advertisements have also appeared on networks used by the United Nations, NATO, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union’s General Secretariat.
‘Almost nobody was watching’
Government networks have also been targeted in at least 24 countries, including the United States, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Australia, Russia, Mexico and Israel itself. Networks of media organisations have also been targeted, mainly in Australia, Denmark and Sweden, according to Citizen Lab.
In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.
O’Shaughnessy said infection has not been confirmed there – only profiling of users. “But that alone is concerning, he said. “The ad system was built to send code from strangers to billions of screens with pinpoint targeting. Almost nobody was watching it from a security angle.”
The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets. “For individuals at high risk, like journalists and officials, the best first defence is to install an ad blocker, switch off their advertising ID through their phone’s privacy settings, keep everything updated, and turn on Lockdown Mode or Android’s Advanced Protection,” he said.
Precautions also need to be taken within the industry and at government level. “To combat this, the ad industry needs to properly vet who’s buying ads,” O’Shaughnessy said, while “regulators need to stop personal data being sprayed out to thousands of unknown bidders in every auction.”
articles.summary:
Researchers have identified a sophisticated "zero-click" spyware campaign by the Israeli firm Candiru that infects devices through malicious advertisements without requiring any user interaction or file downloads.

### Key Points
- Citizen Lab discovered that 45 Al Jazeera staff devices were targeted in June 2025 using spyware that bypasses traditional security by exploiting browser vulnerabilities.
- The Israeli company Discover-Tech facilitated the attacks by posing as a legitimate advertiser to win automated ad auctions and redirect users to infected servers.
- Malicious advertisements were served via major networks including Google, Yandex, and Beeswax, appearing on devices linked to NATO, the UN, and various national defense ministries.
- Once installed, the spyware can capture keystrokes, record microphone and webcam input, and extract sensitive data like emails, messages, and saved credentials.
- The US government previously blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for its role in the illegal surveillance of journalists and activists across 10 countries.

### Why it Matters
This discovery exposes a critical structural vulnerability in the global online advertising ecosystem, which allows malicious actors to deliver code to high-profile targets without needing direct contact. It highlights an urgent need for stricter vetting of ad-tech vendors and improved regulatory oversight to prevent the weaponization of automated advertising auctions.

articles.title: Reolink Home Hub 2 On-Device AI, 16MP Camera Support, and Subscription-Free Security Storage
articles.author: Jude Chukwuemeka
articles.content:
Reolink has launched the Home Hub 2, a next-generation security hub designed to make managing home surveillance footage easier through on-device artificial intelligence, expandable local storage, and centralized camera controls.
Unveiled at IFA 2026, the Home Hub 2 brings Reolink’s ReoNeura AI technology to its home security ecosystem. The device introduces Local AI Video Search, allowing users to find relevant moments in recorded footage using simple keywords instead of manually reviewing hours of video.
The hub also supports a 2.5-inch hard disk drive (HDD) or solid-state drive (SSD), along with a microSD card, giving users additional local storage options without requiring a cloud subscription. It can manage up to eight compatible Reolink cameras from a central location.
Local AI Video Search Makes Security Footage Easier to Find
One of the Home Hub 2’s main features is Local AI Video Search, powered by Reolink’s ReoNeura on-device AI engine.
The feature allows users to search locally stored recordings across connected cameras using keywords. Rather than scrolling through long playback timelines, users can search for relevant footage and go directly to the moments they want to review.
Because the searches run locally on the hub, the feature does not require a cloud subscription. This approach also keeps the search process within the user’s local security setup.
For homeowners reviewing activity around entrances, driveways, gardens, or other monitored areas, the ability to locate specific events more quickly could make everyday security monitoring more convenient.
Cross-Camera Tracking and Upcoming AI Features
The Home Hub 2 is designed to do more than search individual recordings. Its Cross-Camera Tracking feature follows a detected object across multiple cameras and combines the relevant footage into a single video.
This can help users follow activity as it moves between monitored areas, providing a more connected view of an event than reviewing each camera separately.
Reolink also plans to introduce additional AI capabilities through an upcoming firmware update.
These include:
- Custom AI Detection: Designed to let users define the types of scenarios they want the system to recognize.
- AI self-learning: Intended to help the system learn user-defined situations and provide more relevant alerts.
For example, a user could configure the system to recognize a side gate left open. These features are intended to make security notifications more relevant to individual properties, although Reolink says they will arrive in a future firmware update rather than being available at launch.
Expandable Local Storage With Encryption
The Home Hub 2 offers multiple storage options for users who want to keep security recordings locally.
Its storage configuration includes a new SATA slot that supports a 2.5-inch HDD or SSD, as well as a microSD card slot supporting cards of up to 1TB.
This combination gives users flexibility to expand recording capacity according to their needs. It also reduces reliance on cloud-based storage services, which may involve recurring fees.
Reolink says the hub uses encryption to help protect recordings against unauthorized access, including in situations where a camera or microSD card is stolen.
For households that prefer to manage their own surveillance footage, the combination of expandable storage and local AI processing is a central part of the Home Hub 2’s design.
One Hub Can Manage Up to Eight Cameras
The Home Hub 2 supports up to eight compatible Reolink cameras, including battery-powered Wi-Fi, plug-in Wi-Fi, and Power over Ethernet (PoE) models.
It supports cameras with resolutions of up to 16 megapixels and uses 2.4GHz and 5GHz Wi-Fi 6 connectivity.
The hub also creates its own local network. According to Reolink, compatible cameras can continue recording to the hub if the home’s internet connection goes down, helping preserve local surveillance coverage during an internet outage.
Users can manage connected cameras through the Reolink app, where they can view high-definition live feeds and recorded playback across multiple devices.
The app also includes a Regular Security Summary, which presents daily, weekly, or monthly statistics about motion-detection events. This gives users a way to review activity trends and jump directly to relevant recordings.
Camera compatibility and supported features may vary by model, so users should check Reolink’s compatibility information before connecting existing equipment.
App Controls, Time-Lapse Playback, and Custom Alerts
Reolink says the Home Hub 2 can be configured through the Reolink app in three steps. Once set up, users can manage their cameras and review footage from a central interface.
The app’s time-lapse feature can condense longer events into shorter videos. This can be useful for reviewing gradual changes, such as a sunrise or an ongoing construction project, without watching the entire recording.
The hub also features a built-in alarm center that can sound a siren when a connected camera is triggered. Users can choose from available ringtones or select a custom sound.
For additional notification flexibility, the Home Hub 2 supports sending alerts, including images, to Discord, Telegram, and Slack.
The product announcement notes that these integrations are supported, although availability and configuration may depend on the connected services and the user’s setup.
Works With Alexa and Google Assistant
The Home Hub 2 also supports Amazon Alexa and Google Assistant, enabling hands-free viewing on compatible displays, including Amazon Echo Show and Google Nest Hub devices.
This integration gives users another way to check camera feeds without opening the Reolink app each time.
Combined with centralized camera management and local recording, the smart assistant support helps the Home Hub 2 fit into a broader connected-home setup.
No Subscription or Monthly Fees
A key selling point of the Reolink Home Hub 2 is that its listed features are available without a subscription or recurring monthly fees.
Local AI video search, expandable storage, and centralized camera management are designed to operate as part of the user’s own security system. This may appeal to homeowners who prefer to pay for their hardware and storage rather than maintain an ongoing cloud-storage subscription.
The hub’s local network and storage capabilities also offer an alternative for users who want their cameras to continue recording locally during an internet outage.
However, users should distinguish between local recording and remote access: viewing or managing a system from outside the home may still depend on network availability and the relevant configuration.
Pricing and Availability
The Reolink Home Hub 2 is available now in the United States for $199.99.
Buyers can find more information and purchase the device through the official Reolink website.
With support for up to eight compatible cameras, expandable HDD or SSD storage, microSD cards up to 1TB, and on-device AI search, the Home Hub 2 is designed to serve as a centralized management and recording solution for Reolink camera systems.
articles.summary:
Reolink has launched the Home Hub 2, a centralized security management device featuring on-device AI video search and expandable local storage for up to eight compatible cameras.

### Key Points
- The Home Hub 2 supports up to eight Reolink cameras, including Wi-Fi and Power over Ethernet (PoE) models, with resolutions up to 16 megapixels.
- Local AI Video Search allows users to find specific footage using keywords without requiring a cloud subscription.
- Storage options include a SATA slot for 2.5-inch HDDs or SSDs and a microSD card slot supporting up to 1TB.
- The device features Cross-Camera Tracking to follow objects across multiple feeds and integrates with Amazon Alexa and Google Assistant.
- The hub maintains local recording capabilities during internet outages and offers alert integrations for platforms like Discord, Telegram, and Slack.
- The product is currently available in the United States for $199.99.

### Why it Matters
This device offers a subscription-free alternative for homeowners who prioritize data privacy and local control over cloud-based surveillance services. By centralizing AI processing and storage, it provides a cost-effective way to manage complex multi-camera security systems without recurring monthly fees.

articles.title: The bloodletting in stocks is stanched as investors buy the dip and rotate out of tech
articles.author: Jim Edwards
articles.content:
After a grueling couple of days for tech stocks—propelled by drama and speculation around CoreWeave’s debt—traders bought the dip in the past 24 hours, and stocks rose globally. U.S. futures are up before the open in New York, too.
Much of the gains were in non-tech stocks. While the S&P 500 gained 0.33% yesterday, the tech-heavy Nasdaq was flat, and the equal-weight S&P was up a solid 1.36%. “378 names in the S&P 500 were higher on the day,” Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid noted. The index remains within 1% of its record high.
“The selling in tech has been stopped in its tracks, while the rotation into other sectors continues. Tech stocks aren’t out of the woods yet, but rotation of this kind is just what investors need to see, even if it is a deeply painful experience for tech fans,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at trading platform IG, told Fortune in an email.
Words from Warsh did not sound harsh
Investors also listened closely to Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s speech at the IMF—and they liked what they didn’t hear. He did not signal an interest rate rise in October. CME FedWatch futures are now showing an 85% expectation that the Fed will hold rates later this month. (Stock investors generally like it when central banks don’t increase interest rates because it means borrowing costs will remain stable.)
“With Federal Reserve Chair Warsh refusing to give forward guidance on policy at the IMF meetings—then giving forward guidance of a sort. Warsh failed to sound hawkish,” USB’s Paul Donovan told clients this morning. “The word of Warsh carries relatively little weight, but this chimes with [New York] Fed president [John] Williams’s earlier remarks. Expectations for an October rate increase are fading.”
- S&P 500 futures were up 0.42% this morning. The index rose 0.33% yesterday.
- In Europe, the Stoxx 600 was up 0.46% in early trading, and the U.K.’s FTSE 100 was flat before lunch.
- Asia: South Korea’s Kospi was up 2.05%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was up 1.39%. India’s Nifty 50 was up 0.36%. China’s CSI 300 was up 0.11%.
- Brent crude was at $105 per barrel.
- Bitcoin was at $82,101.
Energy stocks hit a 50% gain for the year
Stocks in the S&P 500’s energy sector—buoyed by demand from AI data centers and the rising price of oil—are up 50% year to date, per the Bespoke Investment Group, the first of the index’s official sectors to hit that mark. This year’s rally ranks fifth among all 50% sector gainers since 1990, the group said.

articles.title: IPhone Duo Preorders Sell Out in Minutes: Backordered Until January
articles.author: Dashia Milden
articles.content:
The iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, is a hot ticket.
Preorders for the iPhone Duo began on Friday at 5 a.m. PT, on Apple’s website, the Apple Store app and elsewhere. Although the phone has an Oct. 23 release date, as of now models preordered through Apple won’t ship until the last week of January. The availability at mobile carriers like AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile is more variable. You can also try to buy one in stores on Oct. 23.
CNET Senior Tech Reporter Abrar Al Heeti got to handle the iPhone Duo briefly ahead of preorders, and described it as essentially a compact iPhone that can double as an iPad Mini, well suited for consuming media. Beyond that, she wrote, “It has a satisfying feel and really makes the crease virtually disappear when the screen is on.”
The 7.6-inch screen when opened is the largest iPhone display screen yet (there’s also a 5.4-inch outer display). The Duo is also equipped with two 48-megapixel cameras: a main camera and an ultrawide one. It’s geared for multitasking, with Apple Pencil support and drag-and-drop functionality similar to an iPad.
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999, but trade-in offers and Apple’s Upgrade program could lower how much you pay out of pocket.
Apple is years late to the folding phone market, though that might not matter much to those already in the iPhone ecosystem. The bigger question is whether the iPhone Duo will be tempting to those inclined to buy Android phones, where the latest hinged options include the Samsung Galaxy Fold 8 and Galaxy Flip 8 and the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Apple has officially opened preorders for the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable smartphone, which features a 7.6-inch display and starts at a retail price of $1,999.

### Key Points
- The iPhone Duo features a 7.6-inch internal display, a 5.4-inch outer screen, and dual 48-megapixel cameras.
- Preorders began Friday, but shipping through Apple is currently delayed until the final week of January.
- The device supports the Apple Pencil and includes multitasking features like drag-and-drop functionality.
- Retail availability in physical Apple Stores and at carriers like AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile begins October 23.
- The foldable phone enters a competitive market currently dominated by Samsung’s Galaxy series and Google’s Pixel Fold.

### Why it Matters
This launch marks Apple’s long-awaited entry into the foldable smartphone market, testing whether the company can convert its loyal ecosystem users to a new form factor. The device’s success will determine if Apple can effectively challenge established Android competitors like Samsung and Google in the premium high-end mobile segment.
